symptoms: Small, round, orange-brown pustules scattered on upper leaf surface
Pustules are lighter colored than stem rust
Pustules release rusty-orange spore powder when rubbed
Infected leaves dry prematurely
Grain shriveling if infection is severe during grain filling
cause: Fungus Puccinia triticina. Wind-borne urediniospores can travel hundreds of kilometers. Favored by moderate temperatures (15-25°C) and high humidity. Most common wheat rust in Punjab and Haryana.
treatment: Apply Propiconazole 25% EC at 1ml/litre of water
Spray at first sign of orange-brown pustules
Repeat after 15 days if symptoms persist
Best spray time: evening (4-6 PM) for better absorption
Ensure complete coverage of all leaves
prevention: Plant resistant varieties: PBW 343, HD 2967, WH 1105 (PAU recommended)
Monitor fields from mid-January to March
Early sowing (late October) reduces rust risk
Remove volunteer wheat plants from field margins

recommended_pesticide.name: Propiconazole 25% EC
recommended_pesticide.dosage: 1 ml per litre of water (500 ml per acre)
recommended_pesticide.spray_interval: Single spray, repeat after 15 days if needed

symptoms: Yellow-orange pustules arranged in distinct stripes along leaf veins
Stripes run parallel to the leaf midrib
More prominent on young, upper leaves
Severe infection causes complete leaf yellowing and death
Grain shriveling and significant yield loss if untreated
cause: Fungus Puccinia striiformis. The MOST damaging wheat rust. Favored by cool temperatures (10-15°C) with dew or light rain. Can spread rapidly and devastate entire fields within weeks.
treatment: URGENT: Apply Propiconazole 25% EC at 1ml/litre IMMEDIATELY
This is a yield-devastating disease — every day of delay increases crop loss
Spray entire field, not just visible patches
A single well-timed spray can save 15-20 quintal/hectare
Contact nearest KVK or agricultural university IMMEDIATELY
prevention: Plant resistant varieties recommended by PAU/IARI
Early sowing helps avoid peak infection period
Regular field monitoring from December to February
Report outbreaks to district agriculture officer

recommended_pesticide.spray_interval: Single spray at first symptom, may repeat once

symptoms: Partially converted grain kernels — only part of grain turns black
Infected grains emit strong fishy/rotten smell when crushed
Black powdery mass (teliospores) visible when grain is broken
Mostly affects ear/spike, not the leaves
Often noticed only at harvest
Usually 1-5% of grains affected in a spike
cause: Fungus Tilletia indica (syn. Neovossia indica). Named after Karnal city, Haryana where first identified. Soil-borne. Favored by cool, humid weather during ear heading. India is the country of origin.
treatment: No effective chemical treatment once symptoms appear
Grade and separate infected grain lots
Do NOT use infected grain for seed
Seed treatment with Carboxin 75% WP at 2.5g/kg seed for next season
Deep ploughing after harvest to bury spores
prevention: Seed treatment with Carboxin or Thiram before sowing
Deep ploughing in summer to kill soil-borne spores

symptoms: White to grey powdery fungal growth on upper leaf surface
Can spread to stems and ears in severe cases
Leaves may yellow and die prematurely under heavy infection
Reduced photosynthesis and plant vigor
Small black dots (cleistothecia) may appear in older lesions
cause: Fungus Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici. Spread by wind-borne conidia. Favored by moderate temperatures (15-22°C), high humidity, and dense plant canopy. Common in irrigated, well-fertilized fields.
treatment: Spray at first signs of white powdery patches
Improve air circulation by avoiding excessive irrigation
prevention: Avoid excess irrigation during cool weather
